doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Rehearsing Lonesome Suzie against the producer's doubts
summary: His love for Susan inspired the arrangement; he defended it at CBS rehearsal and later on tour.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Suzie” I was in love with the girl named Susan so-and-so. She ended up in a mental hospital. Unbeknownst to me at the time I was with her, that short time, this was early on in the band. And it’s like Taylor —

“Fire and Rain.” He was in a mental hospital or something, you know, he was, and I think this lady he knew I think committed suicide you know. So I was kind of, not comparing you know, but I was very sensitive, and loved this girl you know, was falling in love, I don’t know. One of my first loves. And so I wrote this arrangement wondering is it okay. I’m using some Bill Evans licks that you hear the horns playing near the end at the climax [scats]. That sounds like Rachmaninoff or Stravinsky or something. It’s very Russian. I have Russian Jew in me. That’s not my religion anymore but I was brought up under that. And [scats] that’s like Prokofiev or something [scats] on “Firebird” there’s a phrase that goes [scats] something like that. So you pick up things. I’m not a classical person but I’m a chameleon like that. So I’m wondering is that okay. So we’re rehearsing in this big room at CBS Records where the orchestras play on famous records. And the producer, I won’t mention the name, for the album, we’re just starting and there’s some intricate stuff there, it’s fairly high, and it’s out stuff. It’s not [scats] like Motown licks, but so Fred’s writing something different. I’m wondering is it okay but it was motivated by inspiration. That lick I was just singing before earlier [scats] that was like I played it very simply at midrange on piano. It’s like a Bill Evans lick. B flat major to D seven to G minor [scats] with a sharp nine in there. Typical for me, I was listening to Bill Evans. McCoy Tyner was my favorite piano player. You know, all these people. So the guy, the producer comes in and the co-producer comes in and he hears people making mistakes with the brass. I mean, this big room. And he said, sort of like a negative attitude like you know, that doesn’t sound so good. Like are we going to drop the horn thing? I said, “Please will you” you know I think you were saying Lew, I wouldn’t settle for, you know, I don’t remember me being like this because I was kind of quiet but if something wasn’t right I would speak up I guess, where I normally wouldn’t as a person but musically, because the force of music is so strong in me, it has to be this way and give it a chance at least. So I said, “Go in your room and give me an hour and let me rehearse this. When I’m through and I’m happy with it if you don’t like it I’ll consider that and you consider that, that’s another story. But don’t break it down right away. You know, what do you know, I’ve spent a whole week on this or whatever. Go into your room. Leave me alone.” And I’ve done this on an Eastern European tour, we played a Yugoslavia, Romania and Poland. And I saw the film of it. It never came out. But we were doing “Lonesome Suzie” and it wasn’t with the producer. Something was messed up and I said, “No, that’s not” you know I got, not angry, but I was the same way again. And it was
funny because I’m very bland, I’m pretty laid back. I don’t yell at anybody. I’m not — I just don’t want to you know. So that’s what happened, I spoke up and I don’t think I’m always like that.
Well it certainly worked, I can tell you that.
